note: The command table: which names an operator or a player may type, and the operation each one runs

information.what: One row per command. `command` is what a player types, without the slash. `also` holds the other names the same command answers to. A row binds its name one of two ways: `execution` names one of the closed chat operations (Teleport, ListTargets, Position) and defaults to the chat surface, or `operation` names a registered operation (for example world.status) and defaults to the console surface. `surfaces` may narrow or widen that: a row may name `chat`, `console`, or both. `parameters` names the values the command takes, in order; an empty list means the command takes none. A name this server cannot run is refused when the file is read, not when a player types it.
information.why this is a file: docs/decisions/0011-the-command-surface-is-content.md and docs/port/14-operator-surfaces.md. The command surface is content: the names, the argument rule and the binding to an operation are facts a server reads, and Rust keeps only the operation. A command is added or moved here without rebuilding the server, and no surface names a command in Rust.
information.where the rows come from: the reference's own two dispatch points - GmCommands.c, which owns /tp, /teleport and /maps, and GmChat.c, which owns /stuck - as the working implementation ports them at ASURA crates/asura-world/src/chat.rs:126-163; the console row is the reference's console name from cs_server.cpp:92
information.not here: the answers a command gives, and the conditions it refuses on. Those are the operation's own, in Rust, until the scripting layer of docs/port/11-content-and-behaviour.md takes them.

commands.doc: a server transfer to the map the argument names, or one of the reference's refusals (unknown map, no config, already here)
